2.1.title: Why does a circuit take time to settle?
2.1.goal: Recognize a transient and identify the energy-storage quantity that changes over time.
2.1.prepare: Recall the capacitor and inductor laws from 1.5.
goals: Tell a switching transient from the final DC steady state.
Explain the three-lamp demonstration using stored energy.
2.1.coverage: The video explains switching and element behavior. The sheet adds your teacher’s lamp demonstration and applications; its microsecond/millisecond examples are not a universal duration limit.

2.2.title: What stays unchanged at the switch?
2.2.goal: Find the state immediately after switching without confusing it with the final steady state.
2.2.prepare: Know the capacitor voltage and inductor current before the switch moves.
goals: Read 0− and 0+ correctly.
Carry uC and iL through switching, then recalculate the other quantities.
2.2.coverage: The video revises continuity and solves RC/RL examples. It also previews time constants from 2.3. The examples below use your teacher’s own circuits.

2.3.title: Build the response from three values
2.3.goal: Find the initial value, final value and time constant, then write and check the response.
2.3.prepare: Use 2.2 switching laws and Chapter 1 equivalent resistance.
goals: Find f(0+), f(∞) and τ from the appropriate circuit.
Use the exponential only when the circuit is first order with fixed DC excitation.
2.3.coverage: The video derives RC/RL responses and the final + (initial − final) shortcut. The sheet keeps the additional initial-value circuits, final-value examples and unit corrections taught in your course.

2.4.title: Charge, discharge or change destination?
2.4.goal: Choose the correct RC response and keep the current sign consistent.
2.4.prepare: Find the three values in 2.3; use iC = C duC/dt.
goals: Distinguish zero-state, zero-input and complete response.
Write both capacitor voltage and current; calculate a threshold time.
2.4.coverage: The video explains RC charging, discharging, τ and a threshold calculation. The sheet adds the teacher’s source-to-source complete response and the passive-reference current sign.

2.5.title: Let an inductor release its energy
2.5.goal: Find the RL decay path, preserve initial current, and explain the voltage sign.
2.5.prepare: Use 2.2 continuity and the resistance seen after switching.
goals: Find the teacher’s 2 A initial current and 0.5 s time constant.
Explain why the current can be positive while the passive voltage is negative.
2.5.coverage: The video covers RL buildup, decay and time constants. It sometimes describes induced EMF or loop traversal drops as negative. Your course’s passive terminal voltage is uL = +L diL/dt; induced EMF is eL = −L diL/dt. Use the marked reference, not the word “voltage” alone.

3.1.title: Read a sine wave before calculating
3.1.goal: Identify amplitude, frequency and phase, and distinguish peak from RMS.
3.1.prepare: Use units, basic angles and resistor power from Chapter 1.
goals: Read Im, ω and ψ in i(t).
Convert peak ↔ RMS and determine which waveform leads.
3.1.coverage: The video covers AC/DC and sine-wave RMS calculations. Its power examples assume sinusoidal in-phase voltage/current; for a general load, use P = UI cosφ in 3.6. The sheet adds your teacher’s frequency and phase material.

3.2.title: Turn sine waves into numbers you can add
3.2.goal: Represent same-frequency signals as phasors and calculate without losing phase or √2.
3.2.prepare: Know 3.1 RMS values and initial phase; use basic trigonometry.
goals: Convert rectangular ↔ polar with the correct quadrant.
Add phasors and recover the waveform using a supplied frequency.
3.2.coverage: The video teaches rotating vectors, mathematical forms and R/L/C phase relationships. It mainly uses peak phasors. Your course calculations below use RMS phasors; the phase angles are unchanged. The sheet also includes the course’s complex-number arithmetic.

3.3.title: Why do R, L and C shift current differently?
3.3.goal: Use each element’s impedance and explain the 90° phase relationship.
3.3.prepare: Use 3.2 phasors and the derivative laws from 1.5.
goals: Write ZR, ZL and ZC with correct signs.
Distinguish phase information from RMS magnitude equations.
3.3.coverage: Khan Academy derives each impedance from its element law using complex exponentials. Its cosine/exponential derivation gives the same impedance laws as your course’s sine reference. The sheet states the phase relationships and corrects the capacitor slide labels.

3.4.title: Add series voltages as phasors
3.4.goal: Find total impedance, current and section voltages without adding RMS magnitudes incorrectly.
goals: Use R+j(XL−XC) and interpret its angle.
Apply the complex voltage divider and verify KVL.
3.4.coverage: The video calculates a series RLC example, reactances, current and element voltage magnitudes. It calls |Z| “impedance”; your course also requires complex Z and the impedance divider, shown below. Its final resonant-frequency calculation is extra to the reviewed lesson.

3.5.title: Add parallel currents without losing direction
3.5.goal: Use the common voltage, add branch-current phasors and apply complex current division.
3.5.prepare: Know 3.2 phasor addition and 3.3 phase relationships.
goals: Explain why three 5 A branch currents can total 5 A.
Get the same answer using branch currents or equivalent impedance.
3.5.coverage: The video works a pure parallel RLC example and checks the vector current sum. The sheet adds your teacher’s general complex branches and current-divider examples. The final resonance calculation is optional beyond the reviewed lesson.

3.6.title: Separate useful power from energy exchange
3.6.goal: Distinguish instantaneous, active, reactive and apparent power, then combine loads correctly.
3.6.prepare: Use RMS magnitudes and φ = voltage phase − current phase.
goals: Interpret positive/negative instantaneous absorbed power.
Calculate P, signed Q, S and power factor with the correct units.
Add P and Q before finding the total S.
3.6.coverage: The first video revisits instantaneous power and derives average power; the second introduces apparent power and power factor. The sheet adds your teacher’s signed reactive power, pure-element cases and addition rules. Capacitor sizing is not part of this reviewed lesson. The videos use peak phasors for some derivations and cosine waveforms; use the RMS factors and consistent sine reference stated below.
